In [[mathematical logic]], '''weak interpretability''' is a notion of translation of [[theory (logic)|logical theories]],  introduced together with [[interpretability]] by [[Alfred Tarski]] in 1953.

Let ''T'' and ''S'' be [[Theory (mathematical logic)|formal theories]]. Slightly simplified, ''T'' is said to be '''weakly interpretable''' in ''S'' if, and only if, the language of ''T'' can be translated into the language of ''S'' in such a way that the translation of every [[theorem]] of ''T'' is consistent with ''S''. Of course, there are some natural conditions on admissible translations here, such as the necessity for a translation to preserve the logical structure of [[Well-formed formula|formulas]].

A generalization of weak interpretability, [[tolerance (in logic)|tolerance]], was introduced by [[Giorgi Japaridze]] in 1992.
